questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Trip production from a survey rate
questions.stem: A household travel survey of the Tarrow metropolitan region in Marovia found that workers aged 16 or over make 2.45 person trips per weekday on average. The region has 620,000 residents aged 16 or over out of a total population of 1,240,000. How many person trips are produced by those workers on an average weekday?
questions.explanation: A trip rate is a per-person rate, so it multiplies the count of the people who make the trips and not the whole population. 620,000 workers at 2.45 trips each gives 620,000 times 2.45, which is 1,519,000 trips. The same product can be split to check it: two trips per worker is 1,240,000 and the remaining 0.45 per worker is 279,000, and the two add to 1,519,000 again. Expressing the same figure per resident gives 1.23 trips, which is the number a modeller would use if the denominator were the whole population; the choice of denominator has to match the rate that was measured.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of workers by the trips each one makes.
questions.learningObjective: convert a per-person trip rate into a daily trip total

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Trip rates by car availability and household size
questions.stem: A cross-classification of Tarrow's 578,000 households records car availability, household size and the average weekday trips each household makes. Car-free households make 2.20 trips a day at one or two persons and 3.35 at three or more; households with one car make 2.80 and 3.60; households with two or more cars make 3.15 and 4.05. The six classes contain 74,000, 31,000, 168,000, 122,000, 95,000 and 88,000 households. Holding household size constant, how much more per day does owning a car add to a household's trips?
questions.explanation: The comparison has to hold household size fixed, because size is itself a strong driver, which is why there are two pairs to read rather than one. Among households of one or two persons, car-free households make 2.20 trips and one-car households 2.80, a difference of 0.60 trips a day. Among households of three or more, the comparison is 3.35 against 3.60, a difference of only 0.25 trips a day. The premium is therefore larger for small households, where a car removes a constraint on a single person's mobility, and smaller for large households, where trips are already made for children and shared errands. Weighting each class by its households gives 1,831,900 trips in the region, a mean of 3.17 trips per household, and the class that contributes most is not the one with the highest rate but the one with the highest rate and the most households, the one car, 1-2 persons class at 470,400 trips. The teaching point is that a cross-classification separates two effects that a single average rate mixes together.
questions.hint: Compare the two rows that differ only in car availability, and do it for each household size.
questions.learningObjective: read a cross-class trip rate table and isolate the car-availability effect

options.text: It adds 0.60 trips a day to a household of one or two persons but only 0.25 to a household of three or more
It adds 0.25 trips a day to a household of one or two persons but 0.60 to a household of three or more
options.misconception: reads the size effect backwards, taking the small premium from the large-household row as if it applied to small households

options.text: It adds the same 0.60 trips a day to households of either size, because car ownership shifts every household by one amount
options.misconception: assumes the car effect is additive and identical across household sizes, ignoring the two distinct rates in each row

options.text: It adds nothing, because the trip totals in the two rows are equal once the household counts are weighted
options.misconception: confuses a weighted regional total with a rate, which cancels only because the class weights are equal

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Net attraction implied by a production and attraction table
questions.stem: An employment survey of the Tarrow region estimates that four sectors of the built-up area produce and attract weekday person trips as follows: Tarrow Central produces 486,000 and attracts 742,000; Belmoor produces 196,000 and attracts 214,000; Keswick produces 158,000 and attracts 121,000; the outer belt produces 260,000 and attracts 23,000. Both columns total 1,100,000 trips. Which sector shows the largest excess of attractions over productions, and what does the excess mean?
questions.explanation: Every trip is produced somewhere and attracted somewhere, so the two columns must total the same number of trips, and they do at 1,100,000 each. The four differences are 256,000 for Tarrow Central, 18,000 for Belmoor, -37,000 for Keswick and -237,000 for the outer belt, and they sum to zero, which is the check that no trip has been invented or lost. The largest excess is Tarrow Central at 256,000 trips: it must be the destination of 256,000 more trips than it generates, which is what a concentrated centre of offices and retail looks like in a matrix. The outer belt runs the other way by 237,000 trips, so it is a net source of trips to somewhere else in the matrix. A distribution step that used these attractions as weights would send most of the outer belt's trips into Tarrow Central, which is the classic direction of a peak-hour commute.
questions.hint: Subtract the production column from the attraction column for each sector and look for the biggest positive value.
questions.learningObjective: find the sector with the largest net attraction in a balanced matrix

options.text: Tarrow Central, by 256,000 trips, and it must be the destination of that many more trips than it generates
Belmoor, by 18,000 trips, and it must be the destination of that many more trips than it generates
options.misconception: picks the second largest net attraction instead of the largest, missing the central concentration

options.text: Tarrow Central, by 256,000 trips, and it must generate that many more trips than it attracts
options.misconception: reverses the sign of the difference, reading a net attractor as a net producer

options.text: The outer belt, by 237,000 trips, and it must be the destination of that many more trips than it generates
options.misconception: takes the largest absolute difference and forgets that a producer has a negative balance

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Fratar distribution with growth factors
questions.stem: A base weekday matrix between three zones, in trips, is 120,000, 100,000 and 60,000 from zone 1; 80,000, 150,000 and 90,000 from zone 2; and 50,000, 70,000 and 110,000 from zone 3. Travel is projected to grow by 15, 5 and minus 10 per cent from zones 1, 2 and 3, and trip attraction is projected to grow by 10, 8 and minus 6 per cent at the destination end. Using the Fratar method, what is the balanced flow from zone 1 to zone 3 in trips?
questions.explanation: The growth factors turn the base matrix into a seed, so the cell from zone 1 to zone 3 starts at 60,000 times 1.15 times 0.94, which is 64,860 trips, and every other cell is treated the same way. Balancing then alternates two scalings: columns are scaled so that each destination receives its projected attraction, and rows are scaled so that each origin produces its projected production. The projected productions are 322,000, 336,000 and 207,000 and the projected attractions are 275,000, 345,600 and 244,400, and both sets total 865,000 trips, so a balanced matrix exists and both margins can be held. After convergence the rows match the productions and the columns match the attractions, and the zone 1 to zone 3 cell settles at 63,406 trips, below its seed because zone 1's total has to be squeezed into a matrix in which the destination that grew least has a claim on it. A useful check on the answer is the ratio within row 1: the seeded ratio of the zone 1 to zone 3 cell to the zone 1 to zone 1 cell is 0.43 and the balanced pair sits at 0.45, so the balancing has moved a little weight towards the destination that grew least, which is the part of a growth-factor method that does not preserve the seed ratios exactly.
questions.hint: Seed each cell with the base flow times both growth factors, then rescale the columns to the new attractions and the rows to the new productions, repeating until both hold.
questions.learningObjective: apply growth factors and rebalance a base matrix with the Fratar method

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Decay exponent fitted from an observed flow table
questions.stem: Between two residential sectors of the Tarrow region, the observed weekday trips fall as the generalised cost between them rises: 12,400 trips at 10 minutes, 6,100 at 20, 3,300 at 30 and 1,900 at 40. A modeller fits a power function of the form flow equals a constant times cost to the power of minus b, by least squares on the logarithms. What does the fitted value of b come to, and what does it say about the strength of decay?
questions.explanation: A power function becomes a straight line in log space, so the fitted slope is minus b and the answer comes from a least-squares fit through the four log pairs rather than from any single pair. The means of the logarithms of cost and of flow are 3.10 and 8.45, the cross-product of the deviations sums to -1.44 and the squared deviations of log cost sum to 1.08, so the slope is -1.44 divided by 1.08, which is -1.33, and therefore b is 1.33. The fitted line predicts 1,580 trips at a cost of 50 minutes, a useful number for a zone the survey never covered. The figure to be careful about is the one produced by reading only the ends of the series: the slope between the first and last point is -1.35, which is close enough to mislead a reader who does not fit, but it is not the least-squares estimate and it uses two of four observations. The observed ratio between 10 and 20 minutes is 0.49, and a decay of about one and a third means the flow at double the cost is about 0.40 of the flow at the lower cost, which is strong decay of the kind produced by a limit on time rather than by habit alone.
questions.hint: Taking logs turns a power function into a straight line, so the fitted slope is minus b.
questions.learningObjective: fit a decay exponent to a flow table and read what the fitted slope implies

options.text: The fit gives b of about 1.33, so flow falls by roughly half for every doubling of generalised cost
The fit gives b of about 1.35, read off the first and last observations of the series
options.misconception: reads a two-point slope between the ends of the series instead of the least-squares fit to all four points

options.text: The fit gives b of about 1.33, which means the flow falls more slowly the further the cost rises
options.misconception: drops the sign of the fitted slope, so a negative relationship is read as a positive one

options.text: The fit gives b of about 1.33, which means each extra minute of cost cancels one further trip from the total
options.misconception: confuses the exponent of a power function with a fixed marginal cost per minute of generalised cost

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why productions and attractions must balance
questions.stem: In a four-stage travel demand model the trip distribution step turns trip productions by origin into a matrix of flows between every pair of zones. What does it require of the productions and the attractions before it can be run?
questions.explanation: A trip is produced by a person in an origin zone and attracted to a purpose in a destination zone, so every trip that leaves the productions column reappears exactly once in the attractions column. The requirement is therefore an identity rather than a target: in a closed region, where nobody enters or leaves, the total of the productions and the total of the attractions must be the same number, and a model that satisfies this exactly is doubly constrained, because it holds both margins. A singly constrained model holds only the productions and lets the attractions be whatever falls out, which is acceptable in a corridor or a study of one side of a city but produces totals that are not defensible for a whole region. The check is cheap and worth running every time a matrix is assembled, because an unbalanced total almost always means a zone has been counted twice, a missing peripheral zone has been dropped, or a boundary has been drawn differently on the production side and the attraction side. An open region adds one more requirement, that the difference between the two totals equals net external trips, which is the one figure a projection cannot invent. Nodal regions with large centres need this discipline most, because they are where productions and attractions are most unequal. That discipline is the reason the distribution step in a four-stage model is a matrix method at all rather than a set of informal rules about which way people travel. It is an accounting device, and accounting devices fail silently. An imbalance of a few per cent never announces itself in the results, and it is only the column totals that reveal it, which is why the same identity is applied in every stage from there on, including in the feedback of assigned link volumes back into the costs that generate the next distribution. Both columns are drawn from the same calendar of journeys, so the identity is not a modelling assumption to be tested but a fact to be enforced, and enforcing it is what allows a later stage to treat the matrix as a set of real journeys rather than as an index. The fact that it can be enforced is the fact that trips have two ends.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to a trip once it has been produced and attracted.
questions.learningObjective: explain the accounting identity behind a trip matrix

options.text: They must total the same number of trips, because each trip has one producing end and one attracting end
Productions must exceed attractions, because every journey begins in a home and ends in a workplace
options.misconception: believes the two columns are intrinsically different in size, so a permanent excess of productions is expected

options.text: They may differ by any amount, because a model can rescale one column to fit the other
options.misconception: thinks a matrix can be made consistent after the fact by rescaling, so no initial balance is needed

options.text: Attractions must equal productions zone by zone, not merely in total
options.misconception: requires a zone-level equality that no trip matrix can satisfy, since almost nobody works where they live

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Generalised cost of a bus journey
questions.stem: A bus journey in the Tarrow region has a 6 minute walk to the stop, runs every 14 minutes, takes 24 minutes in the vehicle and needs no change. The fare is 1.80 pounds and the value of time used in the region is 9.00 pounds per hour. A ticket counts as one third of its face value when it is converted into time. Ignoring the walk, what is the generalised cost of the journey in minutes?
questions.explanation: The generalised cost of a journey is the sum of every minute a traveller spends on it plus the money they pay, converted into minutes at the stated value of time, which here is 9.00 pounds an hour, or 15.00 pence a minute. The average wait is half the headway, 7.00 minutes, because a passenger arrives at a random point in the cycle rather than at the start of it. The fare enters as 1.80 pounds divided by three, giving 0.60 pounds, and that divided by 15.00 pence a minute is 4.00 minutes. The total is then 6.00 plus 7.00 plus 24.00 plus 4.00, which is 41.00 minutes. The same result comes out of pricing the whole journey in money first: 37.00 minutes at 15.00 pence a minute is 5.55 pounds, the ticket adds 0.60 pounds at a third of its face value, and the total of 6.15 pounds divided by 15.00 pence a minute returns 41.00 minutes. Both routes give the same figure, which is the point of converting once rather than twice, since converting the fare at its face value instead would have added 8.00 spurious minutes.
questions.hint: Average wait is half the headway, and divide the fare by three times the value of time per minute.
questions.learningObjective: convert a bus journey description into a generalised cost in minutes

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a generalised cost must add up
questions.stem: A mode choice model compares the cost of driving, of taking a bus and of taking a train between the same two places. Why is the model built on a generalised cost in minutes rather than on a fare in pounds?
questions.explanation: Two of the three costs a traveller bears are not fares. Time is the resource that is actually scarce, and money is convertible into it at a rate the traveller knows, which is why the conversion is defensible where a money-only comparison is not. Generalised cost therefore adds the in-vehicle minutes, the access and egress minutes, the expected waiting minutes, any transfer and interchange penalty, and the fare converted at the value of time with a discount factor that reflects how imperfectly a fare is remembered. Its purpose is to produce one number per alternative that can be used as the impedance in a logit, a gravity model or an assignment. Two things have to be handled with care. Expected waiting is half the headway, not the headway, because arrival is effectively random within the cycle, and the value of time itself is not a constant, since it is higher for a long trip, in the peak, and for a traveller who has no alternative. The conversion factor for a fare, normally a third or a half, is a crude allowance for the fact that a fare is paid once and remembered loosely, whereas time is paid minute by minute. What the model then measures is the generalised minutes that a traveller would pay to save by switching, which is exactly the quantity that has to be calibrated against observed shares rather than assumed.
questions.hint: Two of the three costs are not money at all, so a money-only comparison is not comparing like with like.
questions.learningObjective: identify the components a generalised cost must combine

options.text: Because most of what a traveller gives up is time, so money is converted into minutes and the whole cost is comparable
Because fares are set by operators and are not comparable between a bus and a train, while minutes always are
options.misconception: attributes the need for a common unit to operator fare-setting rather than to the traveller's own tradeoff

options.text: Because a fare in pounds cannot be divided by a value of time without losing the length of the journey
options.misconception: believes a time conversion discards trip length, when in fact the minutes already carry it

options.text: Because money is worth less to a traveller than time, so pounds always understate the true cost of a journey
options.misconception: asserts a fixed undervaluation of money that no evidence supports, since the discount factor runs both ways

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why a withdrawn fare cut does not restore the modelled share
questions.stem: A mode choice model for the Tarrow region is a multinomial logit with a scale of 8 minutes and a fixed alternative specific constant for each mode. A 20 per cent fare cut on buses is modelled by cutting the fare, and the modelled bus share rises from 8.2 to 9.0 per cent. The operator then withdraws the cut and the fare returns to its original value. Using the model as calibrated, what share does it now give for the bus, and what does that imply about how the concession was represented?

answer.exemplar: Holding the alternative specific constants fixed, the model returns the original 8.2 per cent, because the ratio of the bus share to every other share depends only on the difference of generalised costs, and the withdrawal of the cut restores that difference exactly. The gain the cut appeared to buy is not a property of the price; it only ever lived in the constant that recorded it. If the constant had been re-estimated against the observed higher share, the cut would have been written into the constant, and the share would have stayed near that higher figure after the fare returned rather than falling back, because a fare concession that passengers have planned around is not reversed by restoring the price alone. The two behaviours differ in what they assume about travellers: the first assumes the constant is a fixed property of the operator, the second assumes it is a summary of what travellers have learned. The choice is a question for evidence, and the evidence is the observed share after withdrawal, not the arithmetic of the model.

questions.explanation: The model is a constant, not a description of an equilibrium, and the two ways of using a logit give different answers. If the constant is held fixed and only the bus generalised cost is allowed to change, the share depends entirely on the cost difference between bus and every other mode. When the fare returns to its original value that difference returns to its original value, so the bus share returns to 8.2 per cent, and the extra percentage point disappears. If instead the constant is re-estimated so that the model reproduces the observed higher share under the cut, the constant has absorbed the concession, and when the cut is withdrawn the bus generalised cost rises but the constant still credits buses with the discount, so the share stays near the higher figure and does not fall back. That second behaviour is the one calibrated models normally show, and it is a real and useful result: once a fare concession has been in force long enough for people to plan around it, restoring the price does not restore the old share, because the response is not a function of today's price alone. The first reading treats the constant as a fixed property of the operator and its vehicles; the second treats it as a summary of what travellers have learned. Deciding between them requires evidence, not arithmetic, and the evidence is the observed share after the withdrawal. A model that assumes the first will under-predict the durability of any concession, and a model that assumes the second will over-predict the losses from removing one.
questions.hint: With a fixed constant, the ratio of the shares of two alternatives depends only on the difference of their generalised costs.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a logit keeps a fare concession in the constant after the fare returns

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What the value of time does in a mode choice model
questions.stem: A transport appraisal divides a charge of 1.50 pounds on a road by an assumed value of time of 12 pounds per hour in order to express it in minutes of generalised cost. What does the resulting figure of 7.5 minutes represent?
questions.explanation: The conversion says that a traveller who values an hour at 12 pounds treats 1.50 pounds as worth 7.5 minutes, because 1.50 divided by 12 is an eighth of an hour and an eighth of an hour is 7.5 minutes. It is a translation, not an observation: no one spends 7.5 minutes on the toll, and the figure is not the length of the queue either. What it does is make money and time commensurable so that a logit, a gravity model or an assignment can add them. Two features make it crude. The value of time is a distribution, not a point, and it is higher in the peak, for longer journeys, and for travellers with fewer alternatives, so a single figure is an average that fits nobody. And the value of time is itself estimated from choices, which is circular if it is then used to predict choices without care. Its main uses are the appraisal of a charge, the comparison of a fare with a journey-time saving, and the conversion of a time saving into money for a benefit estimate. A toll does not take 7.5 minutes, but if 7.5 minutes is what it costs, then the two changes are tradeable against each other, and that tradeability is the whole point of the exercise. The mistake to avoid is quoting the converted figure as a measured delay, which then feeds back into a scheme appraisal that counts the same minutes a second time.
questions.hint: It is the number of minutes of travel the charge is equivalent to, not a time anyone actually spends.
questions.learningObjective: state the role of the value of time in converting money into generalised cost

options.text: It is the time cost that the charge is equivalent to at that value of time, used so money and time can be added
It is the time actually spent queuing at the toll point, measured over a sample of crossings
options.misconception: reads a money-to-time conversion as a measured operational delay at the charging point

options.text: It is the reduction in journey time the charge buys for the driver who pays it
options.misconception: treats a charge as if it bought a time saving, inverting the sign of the generalised cost

options.text: It is the share of a typical hourly wage that the charge takes from an average driver
options.misconception: substitutes an hourly wage for a value of time, which already includes the cost of not working

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Residuals of a calibrated mode choice model
questions.stem: A logit with a scale of 8 minutes is applied to the Tarrow region with generalised costs of 22 minutes by car, 41.00 by bus and 47 by rail. The observed weekday shares are 86 per cent by car, 8 per cent by bus and 6 per cent by rail. Which alternative does the model most under-predict, and by how many percentage points?
questions.explanation: The model converts each cost into a weight and normalises, so the shares are the exponentials of minus cost over scale, divided by their sum. The car weight is 0.06, the bus weight 0.01 and the rail weight 0.00, which sum to 0.07, giving modelled shares of 88.0 per cent, 8.2 and 3.9. Set against the observed 86, 8 and 6 per cent, the residuals are 1.95 points for the car, 0.18 for the bus and -2.14 for rail, so the model is worst on rail. That pattern is diagnostic rather than merely wrong. A single cost term with one constant per mode cannot express what the rail alternative is worth to a traveller beyond its generalised minutes, and the usual candidates are frequency, reliability, comfort, interchange count and the fact that a rail fare is bought well in advance while a bus fare is bought on the spot. A constant can absorb the average of all of that, but only the average, and once the mode's cost moves the fitted average stops fitting. Two checks are worth making before adjusting anything: the residuals are small enough to be inside the sampling error of a survey of this size, and the ordering of the residuals is systematic rather than random. Rail being consistently under-predicted while car is over-predicted by 1.95 points is the opposite of a constant added at random.
questions.hint: Compute each share with a softmax of the costs, then subtract the observed share from each modelled share.
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a logit by comparing modelled and observed modal shares

options.text: Rail, by 2.1 percentage points, which points at what the cost term fails to capture about rail
Rail, by 2.1 points, which shows the scale parameter has been set too low for every mode
options.misconception: blames a single mis-set scale parameter, which would move all three residuals together rather than one

options.text: The car, by 2.0 points, which shows the model is under-predicting the dominant alternative
options.misconception: reports the largest absolute residual as an under-prediction, missing the sign of the difference

options.text: The bus, by 0.2 points, which shows the fare discount factor has been set too high
options.misconception: blames the fare discount factor, which shifts all bus costs rather than only the bus residual

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a price elasticity of demand states
questions.stem: A regional model states that the price elasticity of car demand is minus 0.35, and the price of fuel rises by 20 per cent. What does the model predict about demand, and what would be wrong with answering in terms of a number of trips?
questions.explanation: An elasticity is a ratio of two percentage changes, so it is dimensionless and it cannot be applied to a count. With an elasticity of minus 0.35 and a price rise of 20 per cent, the demand change is minus 7 per cent, because the two percentages multiply and the minus sign of the elasticity supplies the opposite direction. Applying it to 1.2 million trips gives a loss of 84,000 trips, which is a large number reached from a small proportional change, and the number moves with the base: the same elasticity applied to 240,000 trips removes 16,800. That scaling is the practical reason to work in proportions, since a model calibrated for one size of region can then be used on another. Two cautions follow. The first is that a 20 per cent rise is not small, and an elasticity estimated from small changes is being used outside the range in which it was measured, so the prediction is an extrapolation. The second is that the elasticity of demand for car travel is not the same thing as the elasticity of demand for fuel: a short run sees a much weaker response because journeys cannot be cancelled in a day. A model that reports only the trip total hides both the range caveat and the time horizon, which are the two things that decide whether the answer is credible.
questions.hint: An elasticity multiplies a percentage change to give a percentage change, not a count.
questions.learningObjective: interpret a price elasticity as a proportional rather than an absolute change

options.text: It predicts a fall of about 7 per cent, and the trip count follows only after the change is applied to the base
It predicts a fall of 0.35 trips, and the base is irrelevant because an elasticity is a pure number
options.misconception: reads the elasticity itself as an absolute change in trips, which is the classic unit error

options.text: It predicts a rise of 7 per cent, because an elasticity is defined on the quantity and not on the price
options.misconception: keeps the sign of a cost increase instead of applying the negative sign of the elasticity

options.text: It predicts a fall of 7 per cent, and that percentage is the same in a village and in a large city
options.misconception: assumes a constant percentage rather than applying the change to each base separately

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Car trips after a fuel price rise
questions.stem: The Tarrow region records 1,200,000 car trips on an average weekday. The price of fuel rises by 20 per cent and the model states a constant price elasticity of car demand of -0.35. How many car trips does the model predict for the following weekday?
questions.explanation: A constant elasticity makes the response multiplicative rather than additive, which is what allows a percentage to be applied to a price change of any size. The multiplier is 1.20 raised to the power of -0.35, which is 0.94, and 1,200,000 times 0.94 is 1,125,817 trips. The same multiplier can be obtained by taking logs: -0.35 times the natural logarithm of 1.20, which is -0.06, and the exponential of that is 0.94, identical to the power form to the digits shown. The change is -74,183 trips, which is 6.2 per cent of the base. A check on the elasticity itself: the loss is smaller than the price rise, which is what an absolute value below one means, and it is larger than the change the same 20 per cent rise would produce if the response were linear, which would be 84,000 trips. The gap between those two figures is the whole reason to state an elasticity as a proportion rather than as a slope.
questions.hint: A constant elasticity means the demand multiplies by the price ratio raised to the power of the elasticity.
questions.learningObjective: apply a constant-elasticity response to a base trip total

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Reading a cross-elasticity between two modes
questions.stem: A model reports a cross-elasticity of car demand with respect to the rail fare of positive 0.30. A rail operator cuts its fare by 10 per cent. What does the model predict for car demand, and what does the positive sign tell you about the two modes?
questions.explanation: A cross-elasticity links the price of one good to the demand for another, so its sign is the substantive claim and its size is the magnitude. A positive 0.30 means the two modes are substitutes: a cheaper fare on one pulls demand away from the other. A 10 per cent cut multiplied by 0.30 gives a 3 per cent rise in car demand, and on a base of 900,000 car trips that is 27,000 additional trips, which have to appear somewhere, namely on the road, because the region as a whole is not growing by that much. The negative sign would mean the modes were complements, which is a different model of the world, since a cheaper train that leaves a traveller with more money would raise car use rather than reduce it. The interpretation carries an important practical warning. Because the effect works through substitution, it disappears where there is no competing service, so a fare cut on a line with no parallel road route raises rail use without removing car journeys, and the aggregate benefit is larger than the substitution effect alone. A model that applies the cross-elasticity everywhere will therefore overstate the congestion relief from a rail subsidy, and the size of the error is set by the overlap between the rail catchment and the road network it duplicates. A second warning concerns the range: a cross-elasticity estimated from small fare changes should not be applied to a large one without a check, and the response of car drivers to a rail fare is usually larger than the response to petrol because the rail fare is a discrete purchase that can be deferred or avoided altogether.
questions.hint: A cross-elasticity links the price of one good to the demand for another, and its sign names the relationship.
questions.learningObjective: interpret the sign and size of a cross-elasticity between rival modes

options.text: It predicts a rise of 3 per cent in car demand, and the positive sign means the two modes are substitutes
It predicts a fall of 3 per cent in car demand, and the positive sign means the two modes are substitutes
options.misconception: applies the sign of the price cut instead of the sign of the elasticity to the car demand

options.text: It predicts a rise of 3 per cent in car demand, and the positive sign means the two modes are complements
options.misconception: reads a positive cross-elasticity as complementarity, where the two modes would be used together

options.text: It predicts no change, because a cross-elasticity only links demand to the price of the same mode
options.misconception: restricts elasticity to own-price effects and denies substitution between rival modes

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Why an all-or-nothing assignment overloads links
questions.stem: An assignment loads 30,000 weekday trips onto the network by sending every trip on the least-cost path computed from uncongested link costs. Link a then carries all 30,000 trips, its travel time has risen sharply, and the count taken from the link this morning was lower. Explain what the assignment has done wrong and what the standard remedy adds.

answer.exemplar: The assignment fixed the link costs before it assigned any traffic, so every driver was modelled as if the load it created were costless to anyone else, and no one was allowed to move off the loaded link. That is why link a carries all 30,000 trips and a journey time well above the uncongested one, and it is why the volume disagrees with a count taken on the same morning. The remedy is iteration: assign, recompute every link cost from the volume just assigned, reassign, and repeat until no single traveller can save time by changing route, which is the condition for a user equilibrium. In practice the reassignment blends incremental volume into the path choice, because a deterministic reassignment moves whole classes of trips at once and converges slowly. The point to hold on to is that a converged link volume is a model's attribution of journeys to links and no more; it is only as good as the cost surface and the demand matrix behind it, and a screenline count is stronger evidence than anything the assignment outputs itself.

questions.explanation: The assignment has held costs fixed while it assigned traffic, so it has asked every driver to ignore the traffic the model itself created. That is a contradiction, and it produces a link volume that is too high on the cheap route and far too low on the alternative, because no driver is allowed to move off the loaded link even when doing so is obviously better for them. The remedy is an iteration. Load the trips, recompute every link's cost from the volume just assigned, reassign the trips to the new least-cost paths, and repeat. Each pass shifts some volume from the loaded link to the alternative, the cost of the loaded link falls as its volume falls, and the costs converge; at the fixed point no single driver can reduce their own cost by changing route, which is the condition that defines a user equilibrium. The comparison with the count is the diagnostic that the iteration is needed, because a converged assignment that still disagrees with a screenline total is pointing at the costs, not the paths. Two practical warnings go with it. A purely deterministic assignment flips whole classes of trips between paths and converges slowly, so most practice blends the incremental volume into the path choice so that the load spreads. And the converged volume on a single link is not an observable in its own right: it is a model's attribution of journeys to links, and it is only as good as the cost surface and the demand matrix behind it. A count on a screenline is a harder piece of evidence than anything the assignment produces, which is why validation is done against counts rather than against the assignment's own output.
questions.hint: Ask what a driver facing the risen travel time would do, and what happens if the model assumes the opposite.
questions.learningObjective: explain the failure mode of an uncongested assignment and the iterative remedy

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: How a deterministic assignment splits traffic
questions.stem: Two parallel routes between the same pair of zones have uncongested costs of 18 and 24 minutes, and 400 trips have to be divided between them. How does a deterministic assignment divide them, and what does the answer say about the drivers who end up on the slower route?
questions.explanation: A deterministic assignment does not split the flow in half and it does not put everyone on the cheaper route. It puts a share on the cheap route equal to the cost of the expensive route divided by the sum of the two costs, so here that is 24 over 42, which is 57.1 per cent of the trips, or 229 trips on the 18 minute route and 171 on the 24 minute route. The reasoning is the equilibrium condition: if the costs of the two routes were different once the traffic was on them, some driver would still be able to save time by switching, so the assignment keeps adding traffic to the cheaper route until the two route costs are equal. As it stands, the drivers left on the 24 minute route are modelled as being indifferent, which is defensible only if the assignment is being run on a cost surface that already carries congestion effects. With uncongested costs the two routes never equalise, and the split is an artefact of the rule rather than a prediction. A common wrong answer puts most of the traffic on the cheaper route, on the reasoning that a rational driver takes the fastest path, but rationality plus identical drivers would send everyone to the 18 minute route and overload it. The proportion matters, not the preference: the flow on a link from a deterministic assignment is a number the model chose, and it has to be validated against counts before it is used.
questions.hint: The split is proportional to the cost of the other route, and the reason is that the two costs must be equal at equilibrium.
questions.learningObjective: describe how a deterministic assignment divides flow between parallel routes

options.text: About 229 trips on the 18 minute route and 171 on the 24 minute route, and the drivers on the slower one are assumed indifferent
All 400 trips on the 18 minute route, because a rational driver always takes the shorter of two paths
options.misconception: assumes perfect rationality and identical drivers, so everyone piles onto the cheaper route and overloads it

options.text: 200 trips on each route, because a deterministic assignment divides demand evenly between the alternatives
options.misconception: confuses an even split with the cost-proportional split that a deterministic assignment actually uses

options.text: All 400 trips on the 18 minute route and none on the 24 minute route, which is what a user equilibrium requires
options.misconception: applies the user-equilibrium idea to a pair of routes that cannot equalise on uncongested costs

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: What a volume-delay function supplies to an assignment
questions.stem: A road link has a free-flow travel time of 12 minutes and a capacity of 1,800 vehicles an hour. Why does an assignment for a peak hour need a function relating time to volume rather than a single cost for the link?
questions.explanation: Because a single cost can only be right for one volume, and in a peak hour the volume is what the assignment is trying to determine. A volume-delay function makes the link's cost a function of the load, so the same link carries 900 vehicles at close to its free-flow time and 1,440 at a time well above it, and the assignment responds by moving traffic elsewhere. That is what turns an assignment into a model of congestion rather than a shortest-path exercise, and it is what allows an equilibrium to exist: as traffic leaves a link, its time falls, which keeps inviting traffic back until the costs of the alternatives are equal. The usual forms are polynomial, exponential or logarithmic, and each encodes a different assumption about how badly the link deteriorates near capacity, so the choice is a modelling decision that has to be calibrated against measured times and speeds rather than picked for convenience. A capacity figure alone is not enough either, because it says where breakdown begins but not what travel is like on the way there. The consequence for appraisal is direct: a scheme that adds capacity does not just make the same journeys faster, it lowers the cost of every journey that uses the link, which in a congested network generates additional demand, and any benefit estimate that omits that feedback will overstate the net gain. The function is therefore also where the induced demand effect lives, whether or not it is named there.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the time on the link as the assignment adds vehicles to it, and who bears the result.
questions.learningObjective: state the role of a volume-delay function in a congested assignment

options.text: Because travel time on the link rises with the load, so the cost has to be solved for at the volume being assigned
Because the free-flow time of 12 minutes is a peak-hour average and cannot be used as a fixed cost
options.misconception: attacks the free-flow figure instead of recognising that the cost must depend on the assigned volume

options.text: Because capacity changes through the peak, so the time cannot be read from a table at all
options.misconception: assumes capacity is time-varying, whereas the real unknown in the assignment is the volume

options.text: Because a single cost would let every traveller use the link, so a function is needed to ration the demand
options.misconception: describes congestion pricing as the purpose of the function, which is a policy device applied afterwards

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Route choice on generalised cost
questions.stem: Two routes join the same pair of zones. The minor road takes 50 minutes end to end. The express service has a 26 minute drive, a 30 minute headway, a 12 minute walk to the stop and a fare of 1.80 pounds. A ticket counts as one third of its face value and the value of time is 9.00 pounds per hour. Which route does a generalised cost comparison choose, and by how much?
questions.explanation: Every element has to be in the same unit before the two routes can be compared, and the value of time fixes that unit. The express route's drive is 26 minutes, the expected wait is half the 30 minute headway, or 15.00 minutes, the walk is 12 minutes, and the fare of 1.80 pounds is worth 0.60 pounds once discounted, which at 15.00 pence a minute is 4.00 minutes. The express generalised cost is therefore 57.00 minutes against 50 for the minor road, so the minor road is chosen by -7.0 minutes. The comparison is closer than the raw journey times suggest, because the express service adds a wait and an access walk that the road does not have, and those are exactly the elements a driver would weigh. Note what the three alternatives do: leaving out the walk makes the express service 45.00 minutes and reverses the decision, which is the most likely error because an access walk is easy to forget; waiting the full headway instead of half of it adds 15.00 minutes and makes the minor road win by 22.0; and charging the fare at its face value instead of a third of it adds 8.00 minutes and produces a margin of 15.0 minutes. Each of those is a defensible-looking number produced by a specific mistake, which is why the components should be written out before the comparison rather than after it.
questions.hint: Average the wait, add the walk, and convert the discounted fare into minutes before comparing.
questions.learningObjective: compare two routes on generalised cost including access, wait and fare

options.text: The minor road, which has a generalised cost 7.0 minutes below the express service
The express service, which has a generalised cost 5.0 minutes below the minor road
options.misconception: omits the access walk from the express journey, so the access and egress time is never charged to it

options.text: The minor road, which has a generalised cost 22.0 minutes below the express service
options.misconception: waits the whole headway instead of half of it, double-counting the time a regular passenger does not spend

options.text: The minor road, which has a generalised cost 15.0 minutes below the express service
options.misconception: converts the fare at its face value, which overstates the money cost of a ticket relative to time

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Mode shift after a change in generalised cost
questions.stem: A bus route currently takes 24 minutes in the vehicle with a 1.80 pound fare, a 14 minute headway and a 6 minute walk. A bus lane removes 6.0 minutes from the in-vehicle time, the headway becomes 12.0 minutes and the fare rises by 20 per cent. On the same terms as before, a ticket counts as a third of its face value and the value of time is 9.00 pounds per hour. First work out the new generalised cost in minutes, and then say what a logit with a scale of 8 minutes and unchanged constants would do to the bus share.
questions.explanation: The generalised cost has to be rebuilt from the new terms before anything can be said about demand, because three of its four components move. The in-vehicle time falls from 24 to 18 minutes, the expected wait falls from half of 14 to half of 12, and the fare rises from 1.80 to 2.16 pounds, which is worth 4.80 pence and therefore 4.80 minutes. The new total is 6.00 plus 6.00 plus 18.00 plus 4.80, which is 34.80 minutes, against the 41.00 minutes of the old service, a saving of 6.20 minutes. Two things follow. The saving of 6.20 minutes is larger than the 6.0 minutes taken out of the road, because the shorter headway removes a further 1.00 minute of expected wait, while the fare rise hands 0.80 of a minute of that straight back. And the sign of the shift is set by the direction of the saving, not by the size of the road saving: with unchanged constants a logit raises the bus share whenever the bus generalised cost falls relative to every other mode, and the whole of the 6.20 minutes is available to that comparison. Whether the bus also takes trips from the car rather than from nothing is a separate question that the model answers through its constants, and it is the difference between a mode shift and a service improvement.
questions.hint: Rebuild the generalised cost from the new terms first; the direction of the shift follows from the sign of the change.
questions.learningObjective: carry a generalised cost change through into a predicted shift in trips

options.text: The new generalised cost is 34.80 minutes and the bus share rises, because the bus is cheaper than it was by 6.20 minutes
The new generalised cost is 28.80 minutes and the bus share rises, because the whole 12 minutes saved is available to passengers
options.misconception: credits the bus with the full time saving while also taking the fare increase, double-counting the benefit

options.text: The new generalised cost is 41.00 minutes and the bus share rises, because a bus lane always improves generalised cost
options.misconception: assumes a time saving outweighs a fare rise and ignores the headway change entirely

options.text: The new generalised cost is 34.80 minutes but the bus share falls, because a fare increase outweighs any time saving
options.misconception: presumes the fare increase dominates without comparing the two converted magnitudes on one scale

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Sequence of a congested network assignment
questions.stem: A congested assignment is to be run on a small network so that its link volumes can be checked against a count taken on a screenline. Put the five steps below into the order in which they must be performed.
questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each step needs in place before it can be run. The network has to be loaded before it has any volumes at all, and the first load has to use the uncongested costs because no volumes exist yet; that first pass is a lower bound on the loaded links and the reason the cheap route is over-assigned in it. Once the volumes exist, the costs can be recomputed from them, because a volume-delay function needs a volume and the uncongested cost supplies none. Recomputing the costs is what makes the next pass different, and it is the step that turns a shortest-path exercise into a congested assignment. The fourth step is the reassignment, in which the incremental volume is blended into the path choice so that the load spreads smoothly instead of flipping between paths, and the loop from the second step to the fourth is what repeats until the link volumes stop changing between passes. Only when the loop has closed is there a converged volume set to test, and the test is external: a count taken on a screenline is a measurement, while the assignment's link volumes are a model's attribution of journeys to links. Putting the validation before the convergence step would mean testing a number that is still moving. The whole sequence is an argument about evidence as much as about mechanics, because the count is the only part of the chain that cannot be adjusted to fit the model.
questions.hint: Each step needs the volume or the cost produced by the step before it, so work backwards from the count.
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a congested assignment with validation

options.text: Load the network with every trip on the least-cost path computed from uncongested link costs
options.misconception: must be first because no volumes exist yet, so it is the only pass that can use free-flow costs

options.text: Recompute each link's travel time from the volume just assigned to it
options.misconception: requires the assigned volumes, so it cannot precede the first load of the network

options.text: Reassign the trips to the new least-cost paths, letting volume move off the loaded links
options.misconception: depends on the new costs, so putting it before the costs are recomputed has nothing to reassign to

options.text: Repeat the costing and the reassignment until the link volumes stop changing between passes
options.misconception: is a loop over the two steps before it, so it cannot be entered before they have run at least once

options.text: Compare the converged link volumes with the counts recorded on the screenline
options.misconception: must come last, since a count taken before convergence would be testing a moving number
